items.title: Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 is now available on Google Cloud
items.summary:
Earlier this year, we introduced Gemini Robotics 2 — our next-generation intelligence layer enabling robots to think, act, and adapt in the physical world. At the core of this breakthrough is Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2), a specialized Gemini model that serves as a robot’s high-level brain. Working across any robot embodiment — from stationary arms to full humanoids — Gemini Robotics ER 2 combines advanced spatial and temporal video understanding with long-horizon planning and built-in safety guardrails. This enables robots to converse naturally with humans, orchestrate low-level action models and hardware APIs, execute multi-minute tasks involving hundreds of decisions, and collaborate across multi-robot teams.

Today, we are bringing this same frontier embodied reasoning model to enterprise production environments: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is now available in public preview on the Gemini platform. For the first time, organizations can pair Google DeepMind’s latest embodied reasoning model for robotics with the enterprise-grade security, multi-agent orchestration, and end-to-end lifecycle management of Google Cloud — making it easier to simulate, evaluate, and deploy safe, adaptive physical AI at scale.

Powering physical agents for enterprise robotics

Gemini Robotics ER 2 transforms a robot into a physical agent. The model combines deep spatio-temporal reasoning and long-horizon planning, enabling robots to orchestrate steps to complete a task, self-correct, and generalize to novel situations. To build an agentic setup, developers can declare low-level control interfaces — like Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models or navigation APIs — as tools, and stream multimodal video, audio, or text directly into the model.

Here is what the model delivers for businesses building and operating robotics:

1. Physical task verification, understanding, and self-correction

In physical operations, a robot needs to know whether a step actually succeeded before moving on to the next one. Gemini Robotics ER 2 adapts to new and unfamiliar situations on the fly by reasoning over continuous video feeds. The model:

  • Classifies task progress into binary status, discrete categories, or continuous scores to improve real-time situational awareness and enable real-time adjustment or iteration on failed steps, without restarting an entire workflow.

  • Pinpoints the exact video frame where a critical event occurs (such as when to stop pouring a liquid) with 91.3% accuracy and a 0.96-second mean absolute frame distance, running at 4x the execution speed and a fraction of the compute cost of many larger model categories.

  • It advances our core spatial reasoning capability, including visual question answering and instrument reading. For example, it can read and interpret values across 10+ instrument categories including circular dials, sight glasses, digital displays, linear scales, rulers, and liquid thermometers directly from visual input.

2. One intelligence layer across any embodiments

Gemini Robotics ER 2 orchestrates robots of many shapes and sizes, scaling its intelligence from stationary arms and wheeled rovers to quadrupeds and complex forms. It also unlocks multi-robot collaboration, allowing different types of robots to share a semantic understanding of their workspace, divide labor, and hand off tasks to complete workflows a single machine could not do alone.

3. Agentic tool orchestration and natural language interaction

Gemini Robotics ER 2 thinks about what comes next while simultaneously orchestrating  actions. Developers can declare low-level control interfaces — such as VLA models, navigation APIs, or custom functions — as tools across simulation, real-world robot control, or human tele-operation. Gemini Robotics ER 2 can orchestrate navigation and manipulator movement APIs from natural language commands, allowing the robot to explain its approach while performing an action, and letting operators redirect it without using technical language.

4. Build safe, adaptive physical agents in Google Cloud

Developers and enterprise teams use the Gemini platform to simulate, orchestrate, and manage physical agents, which are then deployed to run directly on physical robots at the edge using Google Cloud's scalable infrastructure:

  • Simulate fast:  Test robot behaviors before touching hardware by running simulations in familiar environments like MuJoCo-Warp and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Then generate synthetic scenarios with multimodal models and auto-label workcell imagery on the Gemini platform.

  • Train smart: Use Gemini Robotics ER 2's spatial pointing, moment finding, and progress classification to curate and label demonstration videos in Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Then train custom Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through the Gemini platform, GKE, or Cluster Director.

  • Operate easily: Deploy Gemini Robotics ER 2 workflows on the Gemini platform with enterprise IAM, security controls, and built-in function calling. Offload latency-sensitive local workloads like SLAM and path planning to factory floors with Google Distributed Cloud, and stream fleet telemetry into BigQuery. Explore the full architecture in Google Cloud Physical AI solutions.

How customers are building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

“We’ve seen exponential growth in customers using AIVI-Learning every month, and Gemini Robotics ER 2 brings them even more value. Video changes what an inspection can be. Spot isn’t just checking whether something looks right in a moment in time, the ability to apply AI models to video opens a whole new world of possibilities.” 

Marco da Silva, VP and General Manager of Spot at Boston Dynamics

“DeepReach AI is the real-world skills engine for physical AI. Our hardware and AI platform capture how skilled people work all over the world, and turn it into data flywheel for model training. Gemini Robotics ER 2 gives us accurate task understanding of every recording, to help us find data that matters most — faster and at a far greater scale.” 

Chris Liu, Co-founder and CTO at DeepReach

“Advanced reasoning models have the potential to help robots interpret complex environments, plan actions and adapt to changing conditions, opening new possibilities for physical AI. Google’s Gemini Robotics ER 2 model represents an important step in this direction, and we’re excited to be working with Google on exploring how these emerging capabilities can shape the next generation of robotics compute platforms.” 

Barrie Mullins, Senior Director of Arm Total Design for Physical AI, at Arm

“We aim to accelerate materials R&D workflows so our scientists can test more ideas, faster. Most lab automation today relies on rigid scripts for single, isolated tasks. By using Gemini Robotics ER 2, we are giving our robots the visual and physical flexibility to work with our existing infrastructure - whether that’s reading a touchscreen on a legacy microwave reactor that has no API, balancing and loading a centrifuge, or moving samples safely through a busy lab. This is the next level that we aspire to reach. This brings us much closer to self-driving labs that can run full experimental campaigns from synthesis to separation, freeing our researchers to focus on thinking up new ideas for discovering new materials.”

Prof. Loh Xian Jun, Executive Director at ASTAR Institute of Materials Research and Engineering (ASTAR IMRE) and Executive Director of MARVEL-AI”

Get started with Gemini Robotics ER 2 in Gemini platform

Developers and enterprise teams can start building with Gemini Robotics ER 2 today in preview via Model Garden in Gemini platform.

items.title: I benchmarked 4 web search APIs for AI agents on 30 live queries
items.story_key: story|title:i benchmarked 4 web search apis for ai agents on 30 live queries
items.content_excerpt: Web search API evaluation for AI agents: You.com, Tavily, Exa and Parallel benchmarked · MCP server on npm & MCP Registry · Claude Code plugin · Hugging Face dataset A web search API evaluation and live, side-by-side benchmark of four web search APIs for AI agents ( You.com, Tavily, Exa and Parallel ) on 30 agent-style queries across GTM, insurance and finance use cases, plus a buyer memo, a target-account list and a market map built on the results. Use the benchmark from wherever you work. Everything is free and read-only; nothing runs on a hosted server with your keys. Ask about these results from inside your AI assistant with the read-only MCP server. It needs no sign-in or API keys and never runs searches. Headline: You.com is the fastest API tested and the most dependable at returning something fresh: it leads on freshness, reliability and search-only speed. Parallel leads accuracy, with You.com a close second and tied on fully correct queries. Exa returns the most on-topic top 5; Parallel is cheapest per correct answer. You.com answered all 30 search-only calls in under 1 second; no other provider managed more than 3 of 10 in any use case. Full scorecards, per-query grids and what each API returned are on the Evaluation page . Queries. 30 queries, 10 per use case (GTM G1–G10, Insurance I1–I10, Finance F1–F10). Each is written the way an AI agent calls web search: Every use case has at least 4 real-time queries; the rest use 24-hour, 48-hour, 7-day or 1-year windows. Some queries expect "none" as the right answer, to test whether an API presents stale pages as current. Same request for everyone. Each provider gets the exact query string with the same parameters: 10 results, full page content where supported, the freshness window, and domain filters where supported. Runs. Searches ran in promptfoo with Python providers: 3 runs per query, 90 calls per API. Latency is client-side wall-clock time around the HTTP request only, on a persistent connection after one discarded warm-up call; provider-reported server latency is recorded alongside. Search-only speed comes from a run of first-time queries sent one at a time, so caching doesn't flatter repeats. Grading. Answers were written and graded from each provider's saved results (top 5), using the published SimpleQA grader rubric for accuracy and FreshQA strict rules for "none" answers and stale results. Answer keys were captured live at run time and archived to the Wayback Machine. Evidence kept per call. R

items.title: A suspended user's agent run still wrote a file: an internal pilot
items.story_key: story|title:a suspended user s agent run still wrote a file an internal pilot
items.content_excerpt: Many permission checks happen when a request arrives. AI agents keep working after that: a run can call tools, wait for an approval and write data well after it started. In an internal pilot, that gap showed up as a file written after the user who started the run had been suspended. The finding: in an internal pilot using Scopehaven's approach, with synthetic data, new requests from a suspended test user were correctly refused, but in 2 of 14 test cases an agent run started before the suspension still wrote a file afterward. In an internal pilot, we used Scopehaven's approach on a pinned version of an open-source AI workspace on our own machine, with its real server, a local model and synthetic data. We suspended a test user. New requests from that user were correctly refused, but in 2 of 14 test cases an agent run started before the suspension still wrote a file afterward. We made a partial, local repair, and the same 14 checks then passed, including the ones confirming that normal use still works. We verified the repair only on the file-write path we tested; other tools and full session termination were not tested. We're not naming the project. This is one finding in one pinned version, reproduced and partly repaired on our machine with synthetic data. It is not a safety certification or a claim about the project's current release. Looking only at new requests, the suspension worked. The file on disk said otherwise. That gap is why, in this pilot, we read the file on disk, not the response to the next request. This section describes a general pattern in agent systems, not that project's code. A web request is usually authorized once, when it arrives, and finishes in a moment. An agent run is different: it can keep working for seconds or minutes, calling tools, waiting for an approval or resuming from a queue. Each of those steps can act on permissions that were checked earlier. The usual remedy is to check the user's current access again right before each action takes effect, not only when the run starts. Whether that holds is something to test, not assume. In each case it is natural to check that the user can no longer do anything new. The question that is easy to miss is what work already in flight does next. Scopehaven is a local assessment workbench for testing the permissions you define, on the actions you check, and rerunning the same checks to show whether a fix held, including the actions that should still work. Runs and evidence stay on your mac

items.title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
items.story_key: story|title:build specialized multimodal models with lfm3
items.content_excerpt: LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. items.story_key: story|title:from spot fixes to measured gains improving document extraction accuracy with ai
items.content_excerpt: How to improve ai_extract accuracy, version prompts and schemas, evaluate results, and how Genie Code can automate them for you Document extraction often starts with a simple loop: spot an incorrect field, adjust the prompt or schema, rerun the document, and check the result. That approach becomes unreliable as fields and document formats multiply. A change may fix one field while introducing regressions elsewhere, work for one layout but fail on another, or appear better simply due to normal variation across LLM runs. We saw this on a recent project that extracted roughly 40 structured fields from partner-submitted order documents across dozens of PDF layouts. Reviewers corrected and approved extracted values before they moved downstream, giving us human-reviewed ground truth for evaluation. The challenge was not getting ai_extract to return the fields. It was improving extraction without degrading the system overall. For example, the revision field sometimes returned status terms such as ORIGINAL instead of a revision number or blank. A small schema change cut errors for that field roughly in half. But across every field, total extraction errors increased by 9%. The lesson was clear: improving one field does not necessarily improve the extraction system. The pipeline already had most of the pieces needed to evaluate changes systematically. Documents landed in object storage and flowed through a Lakeflow SDP pipeline using Auto Loader. Bronze parsed documents with ai_parse_document, Silver extracted structured fields with ai_extract, and Gold published results as a materialized view. Predictions synced to Lakebase, where a Databricks App let reviewers correct and approve fields, and Lakebase CDC returned those approvals to the lakehouse. Two pieces were missing from the feedback loop. Reviewer approvals were available, but they were not assembled into a reusable evaluation dataset. At the same time, prompts and schemas were embedded directly in pipeline code, so even a small change to extraction required a code deployment. We addressed both problems by building a workflow around three questions: What should we change? How should we version it? And what evidence is enough to promote it? Together, these steps create a repeatable path from a proposed extraction change to production, with evidence that the change improves the system as a whole. The rest of this post walks through the practices we recommend and why each one matters. You don't have to implement

items.title: How We Built Our Design Agent
items.summary: How LangChain built Content Studio, an open-source design agent in Slack that makes on-brand videos, graphics and decks, and the harness that powers it.
items.story_key: story|title:how we built our design agent
items.content_excerpt: The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company. This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work. To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things: Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox , integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing. Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design? The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence” . The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. Familiar isn’t always bad, but we wanted our agent to make choices that followed its purpose. Katie Dill , Head of Design at Stripe, makes a helpful comparison

items.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
items.story_key: story|title:can we trust llms to judge whether a research idea is novel
items.content_excerpt: Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. items.title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
items.summary: Deep research, or any use of large language models (LLMs) to read a large document collection and produce insights, requires synthesizing information from different sources. In this work, we find that LLMs produce long-form research reports that read as confident syntheses but which fail to accurately reflect the underlying documents. We call this failure smoothing. In collapsing diverse and potentially conflicting sources into a single narrative, the model discards the evidential "jaggedness" of its corpus and asserts conclusions more decisive than the citations can support. We introduce a claim level scoring pipeline, SmoothScore, to quantify this effect. Our pipeline extracts key conclusive claims from model generated reports, then finds evidence relevant to each claim and clusters that evidence along high level aspects. Finally, each claim is scored with respect to the evidence to quantify the degree of smoothing done by the agent. Across 7 systems and 4 datasets, we find that agents consistently produce stronger claims than warranted.

items.title: Beyond Words Alone: Disentangling Distributed Evidence for Visually Grounded Cultural Translation
items.summary: Social media enables cross-lingual communication, yet the meaning of user-generated content (UGC) is often distributed across text, images, and cultural knowledge, making translation challenging. Existing evaluations typically treat images as optional and assume textual information is sufficient, obscuring whether errors stem from missing visual evidence or inadequate cultural adaptation. We introduce \textbf{Culture-MMT}, a diagnostic benchmark for \textbf{distributed-evidence pragmatic reconstruction} in social-media translation. It contains 498 curated, de-identified UGC instances across 20 domains, categorized into Symbol, Visual, and Hybrid by their required evidence. We also develop a human-aligned domain-specific judge, Judger, and a controlled evaluation framework that systematically varies the evidence available to translators. Across 17 model configurations, real images improve performance by +0.280 on Visual and +0.197 on Hybrid, but only +0.050 on Symbol, while random images provide no comparable gains. Human-authored descriptions further show that jointly dependent cases remain more challenging even when visual facts are explicit. These results characterize culturally effective social-media translation as {meaning reconstruction from distributed evidence}, highlighting visual grounding and cultural-pragmatic adaptation as distinct model bottlenecks.

items.title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
items.summary: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added /claude-api api-version to move Claude API code to API version 2026-10-21
  • Added the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event for each tool call a permission rule, auto mode, a safety check, a hook or the sandbox stopped, prompted or sent back
  • Fixed requests failing with a model-not-found error when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT is set and the model is an alias with the [1m] suffix, such as opus[1m]
  • Fixed the prompt-caching-scope beta header being sent behind custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateways and on Foundry, where it has no effect
  • Fixed MCP servers showing "needs authentication" in claude -p on macOS while the login keychain was locked; they now say why, and the next run after an unlock connects without a new sign-in
  • Fixed MCP servers being reported as timed out, and staying failed in headless runs, when a macOS or Linux computer went to sleep while they were connecting
  • Fixed HTTP MCP tool calls being sent twice when the connection closed mid-call; only read-only or idempotent tools are now retried
  • Fixed a turn sometimes starting without an SDK MCP server's latest tools when a background task was running
  • Fixed some "Autocompact is thrashing" errors in turns that read many PDF pages, images or other large tool results
  • Fixed /autocompact in cloud sessions going back to the default window after the session restarted
  • Fixed a conversation cleared with /clear sometimes coming back when a cloud or self-hosted runner session restarted
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_FIRST_BYTE_TIMEOUT_MS being ignored in Claude apps gateway sessions
  • Fixed telemetry from Claude Desktop sessions behind a Claude apps gateway being rejected when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS is set
  • Fixed /permissions > Recently denied not showing the denied shell command, and auto mode's local classifier ignoring an approval from there when it checks a retried command; approving a row now names the command, not its description
  • Fixed /help and the / command menu showing long model-facing descriptions for bundled skills such as /claude-api instead of their short descriptions
  • Fixed subagent transcripts recording placeholder token usage and an empty stop reason for streamed responses
  • Fixed model switches through the Agent SDK's setModel(), and apps built on it, being refused when the API took more than 5 seconds to confirm the model; Claude Code now waits up to 15 seconds
  • Fixed a background command stopped through a connected app (such as the desktop app archiving an idle session) being reported to Claude as stopped by the user; the notice now names its output file
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions reporting a tool error when a site answered with a 4xx status or a robots.txt refusal; it is now a normal result, as in local sessions
  • Fixed write tools on a directly configured GitHub MCP server showing a form that closed without creating anything in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed Artifact tool reads failing with a connection reset when the server had closed a reused connection
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with --use-anthropic-git-proxy committing a .claude/settings.local.json left in the clone by an earlier session
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session, or stopping the runner, during its checkout hook leaving the hook's processes running and the runner's slot held
  • Improved recovery from unparseable tool calls: Claude Code now retries the call up to twice before ending the turn with an error
  • Improved fork subagents launched together: each is now told which launch is its own, so forks are much less likely to try to start each other's work
  • Improved browser sign-in: the success page now appears as soon as sign-in completes, without waiting for your account profile to load
  • Improved web search errors in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions: a search refused with a 403 that gives a reason now shows that reason instead of a generic "Authentication error"
  • Improved the time to the first reply in cloud sessions when one of the desktop app's MCP servers can't connect
  • Improved Remote Control connect time for sessions whose transcript contains large pasted images or PDF reads
  • Changed the notice Claude gets when the WebSearch budget is used up to also tell it not to query search engines in a browser or through computer use
  • Changed the axScreenReader setting and CLAUDE_AX_SCREEN_READER in a settings env block to apply only from user, managed or --settings settings (since 2.1.305)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed checkout hooks to be stopped after 30 minutes by default, failing the session's setup; if yours needs longer, raise --checkout-hook-timeout-min or set it to 0
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the certificate file built for Anthropic-managed git to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does; a [runner:warn] line gives the number left out
  • [VSCode] Added a notice on the microphone button when voice dictation stops by itself (15 seconds without recognized speech, or the 2-minute limit), saying why and that the text so far is kept
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long prompt expanded with Show more covering the whole chat panel: a pinned prompt is now capped at 40% of the panel and scrolls
  • [VSCode] Fixed part of a list item or table cell with LaTeX math pasting as a new list or table in rich text editors
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation failing behind a TLS-inspecting proxy when NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS is set only in ~/.claude/settings.json; it now also follows CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE
  • [VSCode] Changed the "still open somewhere else" notice to also cover a Claude process left over from an extension restart, which usually ends on its own within about 10 minutes
  • [VSCode] Changed voice dictation to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does
  • [VSCode] Changed the extension's own requests to filter their trusted certificates as the CLI does, and to trust the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file named in the environment or in user settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the repository picker saying "No repositories match" while a search was still running; it now shows "Searching…" until the results arrive
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the "Waiting for a runner" status on self-hosted environments being cut off; with on-demand runners it now counts up from your last message and shows failed attempts
  • [Code Review] Added @claude review stop (also off and pause) to Code Review, ending an @claude review always subscription on a pull request without starting a new review

v0.32.0

Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

  • Structured decisions and generic parsers: the new POST /v1/systemone endpoint answers choice, noul and score questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on Cloudflare/clef-omni (#61064), LiquidAI/d1-3B (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new hf tool and reasoning parser (--tool-call-parser hf, --reasoning-parser hf) reads the checkpoint's response_template, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
  • Low-precision KV cache everywhere: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); fp8_ds_mla on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit ultraquant_4bit KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#57057).
  • Model Runner V2: a GPU n-gram speculator with variable-length drafts (#40704), Elastic EP (#53934), pipeline parallelism with prefill context parallelism for MLA models (#59139), a stock torch.compile mode (#59079), and MRV2 is now the default on ROCm with the model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360).
  • Faster startup and serving: vllm download-kernels installs FlashInfer's precompiled kernels (#58765); vllm preload --preload-autotune keeps the FlashInfer autotune table warm across restarts (#60085); a shared-memory tensor arena broadcasts large multimodal tensors to workers with one copy (#51207); tokenizers and processors load from the local snapshot (#60825); and with --api-server-count above 1 each connection goes to the least-loaded API worker, for 43-85% more req/s on short requests (Qwen3-0.6B, 32 input / 1 output tokens) in the PR's benchmark (#60723).
  • Model support: new EmbeddingGemma 2 omni-modal embeddings (#60254), MiniCPM-V 4.7 (#58674) and Nemotron 3.5 ASR (#59827); video input in the Transformers modeling backend (#57441); GLM-5.3 sparse MLA index conversions reused across layers (3.5-3.9x on that kernel, #59464) and fused multi-step draft decode (13.3% at concurrency 1, #57443); HiSparse per-request residency caching for up to 58% more throughput on GLM-5.3-NVFP4 on B200 with long, fully GPU-resident contexts at high concurrency (#60083).
  • Security: fixes for GHSA-4hhp-h66f-j5j7 (chat template resource exhaustion, #50300), GHSA-q97c-p368-75c4 (tokenizer max_token_id, #59491) and GHSA-frvg-qw88-hww9 (P2P ZMQ socket exhaustion, #51504); CORS no longer allows every origin by default (#61009); untrusted images are limited to raster formats (#60022); shared-memory multimodal cache handles are signed (#59357); and JSON schemas nested deeper than 64 levels are rejected (#60036).
  • Breaking changes: Python 3.10 dropped (#60402); default CORS origins restricted (#61009); transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 and tokenizers>=0.23.2 (#57387, #59796); torch.compile sequence parallelism and AsyncTP passes removed (#60517); cascade attention removed (#61126); mamba_cache_mode="all" removed (#58997); max_tokens no longer reserved from the context window (#57035); Responses API reasoning stream events renamed (#59652).

Breaking Changes & Deprecations

  • Python 3.10 is no longer supported; the minimum is Python 3.11 (#60402).
  • Default CORS origins changed from * to none; set --allowed-origins for browser clients (#61009).
  • transformers>=5.16.1,<5.20.0 and tokenizers>=0.23.2 are required (#57387, #59796).
  • The torch.compile sequence parallelism and AsyncTP passes were removed, along with PassConfig.enable_sp, fuse_gemm_comms and sp_min_token_num; model-level sequence parallelism is unaffected (#60517).
  • Cascade attention was removed; --disable-cascade-attn still parses but only warns and will be removed in v0.33.0 (#61126).
  • mamba_cache_mode="all" was removed; --mamba-cache-mode all now fails validation (#58997).
  • Previously deprecated APIs were removed: wait_for_inflight_requests (use mode="wait"), AsyncLLM.pause_generation(), IOProcessor.output_to_response, vllm.scripts.main() and vllm bench throughput --dataset (#60923). The sonnet benchmark dataset was removed as scheduled (#60129). Tensorizer support was removed from LoRA (#60024), and the PyO3 vllm._rust_tool_parser bridge was removed (#59744).
  • API changes: max_tokens is treated as an upper bound on output rather than reserved from the context window (#57035); Responses API streaming uses response.content_part.added/done with part.type="reasoning_text" instead of response.reasoning_part.added/done (#59652); SamplingParams.prompt_logprob_token_ids is per row (#56984); /inference/v1/generate logprobs use integer token IDs (#58181); sleep API responses are standardized and invalid levels return 400 (#52864); return_mm_kwargs is deprecated in favor of mm_payload (#61427).
  • Watermarking: when the engine has watermarking configured, an omitted request field means enabled and only false opts out; unsupported combinations warn and fall back (#56801).
  • Rust frontend: qwen3_xml now parses Qwen3-Coder XML (alias of qwen3_coder); use the new qwen3_json for the JSON format (#60136).
  • New defaults: shared-memory tensor arena on (#51207); GLM-5.x FP8 KV cache on SM100 with --kv-cache-dtype auto (#60140, #60281); VLLM_DEEPEP_V2_ALLOW_HYBRID_MODE=1 (#57991); Humming preferred over Marlin on SM90 (#56997); sparse_mla_prefill_workspace_factor 2 above 256K max_model_len (#61023); MRV2 on ROCm with model-specific MRV1 exceptions removed (#56360); VLLM_ROCM_AITER_MLA_DCP_VERIFY=auto (#59965); dtype=auto picks bfloat16 on PowerPC (#58528); MXFP4 W4A4 checkpoints fall back to W4A16 with a warning when no W4A4 kernel exists (#60079).
  • Stricter validation: incompatible --prefix-match-unit (#58021), max_num_scheduled_tokens=0 (#60714), HiSparse with cudagraph_mode=FULL (#59688), and negative --device-ids (#49053) are rejected at startup.
